idiom_name: data-only carrier type + single assembler + transport serializer
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare a data-only type holding exactly the fields the boundary consumer needs, with no behaviour beyond transport conventions; keep exactly one assembler that builds it from domain objects and rebuilds domain objects from it, and let the transport serializer encode it. Decide the wire shape deliberately (field names, optionality, absence semantics) and version it, keeping the domain object graph strictly inside the boundary. Where the language allows, make the carrier immutable, and generate it from a schema as soon as more than one team or language consumes the payload.
code_sketch:
dto = Dto(field_a, field_b, optional_c)   # data only, serializable
facade.call(dto)                          # one coarse-grained call

# far side:
domain = assembler.to_domain(dto)         # the only place that knows both shapes
domain.execute()
pitfalls: Serializing the domain object graph instead of an assembled carrier: lazy references, cycles and internal fields escape the boundary.
A carrier shared by several call sites with near-identical fields, so the shape drifts and no one owns the contract.
Mapping implemented in the callers instead of one assembler, so the two directions disagree.
Bidirectional entity relationships (e.g., Order→Customer→Orders) cause infinite recursion during JSON serialization unless one side carries @JsonIgnore or a dedicated non-recursive DTO is used.
Mapping outside a transaction boundary when the entity has lazy-loaded associations: LazyInitializationException fires after the session closes.

Reflection-based mapper silently skipping unmapped fields: configure unmappedTargetPolicy = ReportingPolicy.ERROR (MapStruct) or modelMapper.getConfiguration().setFieldMatchingEnabled(true) to catch drift.
Reusing or renumbering protobuf field tags after publishing: old clients reading new binary see wrong fields; always add new tags and deprecate old ones.

Fetching JPA entities then mapping to DTOs loses the performance benefit of direct DTO projections: use JPQL constructor expressions, TupleTransformer, or native query result set mapping instead (Thorben Janssen, thorben-janssen.com).
DTO explosion: a unique DTO per screen/endpoint with near-identical fields causes mapping duplication and no single owned contract.
Using the same DTO for create, read, update and delete conflates mutable input, immutable output and server-controlled fields, making the contract incoherent and the boundary leaky.
Mutable DTOs as shared state: public setters let any holder rewrite the payload in transit, destroying encapsulation.
Validation leaks into the wrong layer: putting domain invariants in the DTO blurs the boundary; DTOs enforce shape (nullability, format, range), domain enforces business rules.
Over-fetching via ORMs for DTO projections: loading full aggregate roots when only a subset of columns is needed; specify exactly the columns in the query projection.

Wrong move: binding request bodies straight onto persistence entities (the pre-DTO state of the ASP.NET Core minimal-API tutorial) -> clients set server-controlled fields like Id, audit columns or isAdmin (over-posting) -> instead accept a dedicated input DTO exposing only client-editable properties and map to the entity before persisting.

Wrong move: reflexively adding a DTO layer plus Dozer/ModelMapper on top of a lightweight ORM stack -> conversion overhead, mapper configuration and schema-change maintenance exceed any benefit and the DTO becomes pure ceremony (Frankel, 'DTO in anger') -> instead fetch unmanaged DTO projections directly (JPQL constructor expressions, TupleTransformer) or hand-write the mapper at real boundaries only.

Wrong move: mirroring every domain object into DTOs inside a single-process design -> getters/setters proliferate and the domain decays into anemic data bags, violating encapsulation (Yegor256's 'Data Transfer Object Is a Shame' critique) -> instead keep behaviour in the domain objects and create carriers only where a real boundary (remote call, message, published API) exists.

https://matthiasnoback.nl/2022/09/is-it-a-dto-or-a-value-object/ — Matthias Noback: DTO declares a schema (names+types) with no value guarantees; Value Object provides evidence of correctness via invariants; clear decision table.
https://madewithlove.com/blog/value-objects-vs-dtos/ — Bram Devries: pragmatic DTO vs VO decision, validation belongs to the layer that owns the rules.

https://thorben-janssen.com/object-mapper-dto/ — Thorben Janssen: why fetching entities then mapping to DTOs discards the performance benefit of DTO projections; use JPQL constructor expressions, TupleTransformer, ResultTransformer for direct instantiation.
